description: This topic forms the foundational framework of Physics. It covers the study of Physical Quantities, their standard Units, and Dimensional Formulas, which are highly crucial for rote memorization and conceptual clarity in competitive exams.

sections.title: Physical Quantities and their Types
sections.description: Physical quantities are properties of a material or system that can be quantified by measurement. Physics laws are expressed in terms of these quantities.

key_concepts.explanation: Quantities that are completely independent of each other and cannot be expressed in terms of other quantities (e.g., Mass, Length, Time).
Quantities that are derived using two or more fundamental quantities (e.g., Velocity, Force, Work, Volume).
Physical quantities that have only magnitude and no direction. They follow simple algebraic rules of addition. Examples: Distance, Speed, Mass, Work, Temperature.
Physical quantities that possess both magnitude and direction and strictly obey the laws of vector addition. Examples: Displacement, Velocity, Acceleration, Force, Momentum.

sections.title: Systems of Units
sections.description: Various systems of units have been used globally to standardise the measurement of physical quantities.

key_concepts.explanation: In this system, Length is measured in Centimeter, Mass in Gram, and Time in Second.
In this system, Length is measured in Meter, Mass in Kilogram, and Time in Second.
Adopted in 1960, it is the modern and extended version of the MKS system. It globally standardizes measurements into 7 fundamental units and 2 supplementary units.

important_facts.fact: The 7 Fundamental SI Units are: Meter (Length), Kilogram (Mass), Second (Time), Kelvin (Temperature), Ampere (Electric Current), Candela (Luminous Intensity), and Mole (Amount of Substance).
The 2 Supplementary SI Units are: Radian (used to measure Plane Angle) and Steradian (used to measure Solid Angle).

sections.title: Important Derived Quantities and their Units
sections.description: These are highly tested SI units of derived physical quantities, often asked in matching or direct one-liner formats.

key_associations.extra_info: CGS Unit is Dyne. $1 Newton = 10^5 Dyne$
CGS Unit is Erg. $1 Joule = 10^7 Erg$
Another practical unit is Horsepower (HP). $1 HP = 746 Watts$
$1 Pascal = 1 N/m^2$. Also measured in Bar ($1 Bar = 10^5 Pa$).
The unit for Electrical Conductance is Mho or Siemens.
Represents the number of oscillations or cycles per second.

sections.title: Dimensions and Dimensional Formulas
sections.description: Dimensions are the powers to which fundamental units are raised to express a derived physical quantity.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: The dimensions of all the terms on both sides of a physical equation must be identically the same.
scientific_principles.application: Used strictly to check the dimensional correctness of physical equations and derive relations among physical quantities.

key_associations.extra_info: Derived from Force × Displacement. (Note: Work and Torque share the same dimension).
Derived from Newton's Law of Gravitation: $F = G(m_1 m_2)/r^2$.

sections.title: Important Scientific Measuring Instruments
sections.description: Crucial scientific instruments and their direct applications, frequently asked in static GK sections.

key_associations.extra_info: A sudden drop in barometer reading indicates an approaching storm.
Measures the moisture content present in the atmosphere.
Works on the principle of specific gravity to determine water content in milk.
Utilizes the reflection of sound waves (echo) to measure ocean depth.
Records seismic waves; intensity is measured on the Richter Scale.

sections.title: Units of Astronomical Distances
sections.description: Specialized units used in astronomy to measure massive distances between celestial bodies.

important_facts.fact: Light Year: The distance traveled by light in a vacuum in one Earth year. $1 Light Year = 9.46 \times 10^{15} meters$. (Note: It is a unit of Distance, NOT Time).
Parsec (Parallactic Second): The largest practical unit of distance used in astronomy. $1 Parsec = 3.26 Light Years$.
Astronomical Unit (AU): The mean distance between the center of the Earth and the center of the Sun. $1 AU = 1.496 \times 10^{11} meters$.
